items.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007
items.q: In one of mine — an early band that I was in we had a guy named Walter Bow, a young black guy of our generation who was our regular trumpet player.

ctx.x: When you go to the jazz parties now that play I guess what we would call classic jazz, you see very few black musicians playing at these parties.

There are very few black musicians playing this kind of music. Where you will find them is in New Orleans where you’ll find some blacks saying hey this is our heritage why aren’t we playing this and then they do start to play it. But I’ve played certainly with black players, I’ve had them in bands that I’ve been in. I’ve played with Manzie Johnson who was with — I think played with Louis and he also played with Jelly Roll Morton. I’ve played Arvell Shaw who was with Louis. I’ve played with — well you know,…

We’re going to be running out of tape soon. But this is a great conversation. I wanted to — a couple of things you wrote, one thing I really just want to say is a great little description you wrote of the sixth chorus on Ellington’s recording of “Koko,” you described it as “sounds as if we were opening and closing a door on a cocktail party.”
